questions.question: Beyond determining how software is written, what else does the choice of data model profoundly shape?

options.text: How we think about the problem we are solving
How the storage engine lays out bytes on disk
How many machines the finished system will need
Which query optimizer the database can use

questions.explanation: A data model is not only an implementation detail: it supplies the concepts (tables and rows, nested documents, vertices and edges) through which engineers frame the problem itself. The same domain looks different when viewed as relations, as self-contained documents, or as a graph, so the choice influences which solutions seem natural. Physical byte layout, machine count, and the optimizer are decided at other layers, by the storage engine and deployment, not by the abstract model.

questions.question: A data model has two distinct effects on the work of building software. Which two? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: How the software is written
How we think about the problem we are solving
How fast the hardware executes queries
How much disk the data consumes

questions.explanation: A data model shapes both implementation and thought. It determines the structures and operations code naturally expresses, and it also provides the vocabulary in which engineers understand the problem; changing models can therefore change both code and reasoning.

optionExplanations.a: A data model determines the structures, relationships, and operations that application code can express naturally. Changing the model therefore changes interfaces and implementation even when the underlying facts stay the same.
optionExplanations.b: A model supplies the concepts and vocabulary used to frame the domain, so it shapes reasoning before code is written. A graph, document, and relational view can make different aspects of the same problem salient.
optionExplanations.c: Hardware and query-engine implementation largely determine execution speed; choosing a model does not mechanically set the CPU's performance. A poor model fit may cause inefficient queries, but that is an indirect workload interaction.
optionExplanations.d: Encoding and storage layout affect bytes consumed, while the abstract data model alone does not fix physical size. The same relational or document data can be encoded with very different overheads.

questions.question: Most applications are built by layering one data model on another. What is the single key question you ask at each layer?

options.text: How fast can this particular layer be made to run?
How is it represented in terms of the next-lower layer?
Which team owns and operates this particular layer?
Can this layer be replaced independently of the others?

questions.explanation: At every layer, ask how its concepts are represented using the layer below—for example, application objects as JSON, JSON as bytes, and bytes as electrical or magnetic state. A good abstraction hides lower-level complexity while preserving the operations the upper layer needs.

questions.question: Applications layer one data model on another. Order these layers of data representation from highest (closest to the application) to lowest.

options.text: Application objects; a general-purpose model; bytes; electrical currents
A general-purpose model; application objects; bytes; electrical currents and light
Bytes on disk; application objects; a general-purpose model; electrical currents
Electrical currents; bytes on disk; a general-purpose model; application objects

questions.explanation: The application developer models the real world as application-specific objects and data structures; those are stored using a general-purpose data model such as JSON documents, relational tables, or a graph; the database engine represents that model as bytes in memory, on disk, or on the network; and hardware represents bytes as electrical currents, pulses of light, or magnetic fields. Each layer hides the complexity of the layer below behind a cleaner model, so the order runs from most application-specific to most physical.

questions.question: What organizational benefit comes from layering data models?

options.text: It reduces the number of engineers needed, since one team can own every layer
Vendor engineers and application developers can work together effectively
It makes the resulting system measurably faster at runtime in production
It removes the need to document the interfaces between the teams

questions.explanation: Each layer exposes a clean data model that hides the complexity beneath it. Because of that boundary, database-vendor engineers can work on how a model is stored as bytes while application developers work against the model without knowing those internals. Layering does not by itself make a system faster or remove the need to understand interfaces; its benefit is a workable division of labour between groups of people.

questions.question: Every data model embodies assumptions about how it will be used. Which consequences follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some kinds of usage are easy, others are not supported
Some operations are fast, others perform badly
Some data transformations feel natural, others are awkward
Some models are free, others require commercial licensing

questions.explanation: A model makes some relationships and operations natural while making others awkward or slow. Choosing a model is therefore a workload decision: it should fit the application's common access patterns and expected evolution, not merely store the current data shape.

optionExplanations.a: Every model privileges particular relationships and access patterns, so some queries map directly to its primitives while others may not be supported. This is why model selection must follow the intended workload.
optionExplanations.b: Operations aligned with a model's indexes and structure can be efficient, while mismatched access patterns require scans, joins, or application work. A model is therefore also a performance choice.
optionExplanations.c: Tree-shaped documents make nested one-to-many data natural, while dense cross-links are often more natural in graphs or relations. The awkwardness reflects the model's assumptions rather than an inability to store the bytes.
optionExplanations.d: Licensing is a property of a product and vendor, not of the relational, document, or graph model itself. Open-source and commercial implementations exist for several models.

questions.question: What is the difference between choosing a data model and choosing a storage engine?

options.text: The model is a vendor product choice; the engine is a query language choice made later
The model is how you express and query data; the engine is how bytes are laid out
The model fixes the on-disk layout; the engine decides which joins are allowed
They are two names for one decision, taken at two different points in time

questions.explanation: A data model — relational, document, graph — is the layer you write the application against. Storage and retrieval is one layer down: how that model is represented in bytes. The same model can sit on very different engines, which is exactly why the two decisions separate.

questions.question: In Codd's relational model, what are relations and tuples called in SQL, and how are the tuples within a relation organized?

options.text: Relations are tables and tuples are rows; a relation's tuples are unordered
Relations are rows and tuples are tables; a relation is an ordered list of tuples
Relations are schemas and tuples are columns; tuple order is significant to queries
Relations are indexes and tuples are keys; tuples are kept sorted by key

questions.explanation: Edgar Codd proposed the relational model in 1970: data is organized into relations (SQL tables), each of which is an unordered collection of tuples (SQL rows). Unorderedness matters because a query cannot depend on the physical sequence of rows, which leaves the database free to store, move, and scan rows in whatever order is efficient. Columns are attributes of a relation, not tuples, and sorted order is a property of an index rather than of a relation.

questions.question: Which workloads were relational databases originally built to serve?

options.text: Scientific simulation on supercomputers
Real-time telemetry from scientific instruments
Mainframe business transactions and batch processing
Early web applications such as online publishing and e-commerce

questions.explanation: Relational databases grew out of business data processing on 1960s and 1970s mainframes: transaction processing (sales and banking transactions, airline reservations, warehouse stock-keeping) and batch processing (invoicing, payroll, reporting). Web applications came decades later; the notable point is that the model then generalized well to online publishing, social networking, e-commerce, and many other uses far beyond its original scope.

questions.question: Before the relational model, what did other databases force application developers to think about, which the relational model set out to hide?

options.text: The internal representation of the data inside the database
The exact SQL syntax that each database vendor accepted
Manually beginning and committing every single transaction
Sharding their data across several machines by hand as it grew

questions.explanation: Databases of that era, such as hierarchical and network (CODASYL) systems, exposed how records were physically structured and linked, so application code had to navigate that internal representation. The relational model's goal was to hide this implementation detail behind a cleaner interface: tables of rows queried by condition. SQL itself came with the relational model, so it could not have been the earlier burden, and manual sharding is a much later scalability concern.

questions.question: Which timeline correctly places these competitors to the relational model: the network and hierarchical models, object databases, and XML databases?

options.text: Network/hierarchical 1970s-early 80s; object databases late 80s-early 90s; XML early 2000s
Object databases in the 1970s; network/hierarchical in the 1990s; XML in the 2010s
XML in the 1980s; object databases in the 1990s; network/hierarchical in the 2000s
All three of them emerged together during the 1990s and competed directly

questions.explanation: The network (CODASYL) and hierarchical (IMS) models were the main alternatives in the 1970s and early 1980s; object databases came and went in the late 1980s and early 1990s; XML databases appeared in the early 2000s but saw only niche adoption. Each challenger generated hype in its time but did not displace relational databases, which is the backdrop for judging later NoSQL claims.

questions.question: As computers became vastly more powerful, networked, and used for increasingly diverse purposes, what happened to relational databases?

options.text: They were largely displaced by object databases for new kinds of workload
They generalized well beyond business data processing to many other uses
They stayed confined to the mainframe business data processing they began with
They survived mainly through vendor lock-in created by SQL standardization

questions.explanation: Relational databases, designed for business data processing, turned out to generalize remarkably well: online publishing, discussion, social networking, e-commerce, games, and software-as-a-service applications were still largely powered by them. Object databases came and went, and lock-in alone does not explain adoption across so many new domains; the model's generality does.

questions.question: Where did the name 'NoSQL' actually come from?

options.text: A 1998 research paper proposing non-relational storage for the web
A 2009 Twitter hashtag for a meetup, later reread as 'Not Only SQL'
A marketing campaign run by the makers of MongoDB
An internal Google codename that leaked into public use

questions.explanation: The name began as a 2009 Twitter hashtag for a meetup about open-source, distributed, nonrelational databases. It was later reinterpreted as “Not Only SQL,” a more useful label because these systems are defined by varied goals rather than a single rejection of SQL.

questions.question: Which forces drove NoSQL adoption? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A need for greater scalability — very large datasets or very high write throughput
A widespread preference for free and open source over commercial products
Specialized query operations the relational model supports poorly, and schema frustration
A shortage of engineers who knew SQL well enough to use relational databases

questions.explanation: Four driving forces are usually cited: a need for greater scalability (very large datasets or very high write throughput), a preference for free and open-source software over commercial products, specialized query operations that the relational model supports poorly, and frustration with restrictive relational schemas together with a desire for a more dynamic, expressive model. A lack of SQL skills was not among them; SQL was the widespread, familiar option.

optionExplanations.a: Some NoSQL systems targeted datasets and write rates that were difficult or expensive to handle with the relational products then in use. Horizontal scale and high throughput were explicit adoption drivers.
optionExplanations.b: Many teams preferred freely available open-source systems over expensive commercial database products. That organizational and economic preference contributed to adoption independently of data modeling.
optionExplanations.c: Specialized access patterns and frustration with rigid relational schemas encouraged systems with different query models and schema flexibility. The force was not that relations were useless, but that some workloads fit poorly.
optionExplanations.d: A shortage of SQL knowledge is not identified as a driver; SQL was already widespread and well understood. NoSQL systems often introduced unfamiliar APIs, so they did not simply solve a training shortage.

questions.question: What does the term polyglot persistence describe, and what reasoning supports it?

options.text: Relational and nonrelational stores coexist, because each application's needs differ
Every application should settle on exactly one database chosen carefully up front
All data should eventually migrate to a single polyglot engine that speaks every model
Applications should speak several query languages against one shared store

questions.explanation: Polyglot persistence is the expectation that relational databases will continue to be used alongside a broad variety of nonrelational datastores. The reasoning is that different applications have different requirements, so the best technology for one use case may be different from the best for another. It is about several stores, each chosen for its fit, not about one engine that speaks many languages or one database chosen for everything.

questions.question: The mismatch between application objects and relational tables is called an 'impedance mismatch', a term borrowed from electronics. What does the term mean in electronics?

options.text: Impedance is just resistance, so the term means a connection that runs slowly
Power transfer peaks when impedances match; a mismatch causes signal reflections
It means a voltage difference between two components that share one power supply
It is a mechanical-engineering term for friction between two moving parts

questions.explanation: Every circuit has an impedance (resistance to alternating current) at its inputs and outputs. When one circuit's output feeds another's input, power transfer is maximized when the two impedances match; a mismatch leads to signal reflections and other trouble. In databases the analogue is the awkward translation layer needed between objects in application code and the tables, rows, and columns of the relational model: two models that do not fit cleanly at their connection point.

questions.question: What do object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks such as ActiveRecord and Hibernate achieve, and what can they not do?

options.text: They cut translation boilerplate but cannot fully hide the differences between the models
They fully eliminate the impedance mismatch, so applications never see tables or rows
They replace the relational database underneath with a native object store
They translate reads into objects but cannot be used to write data back

questions.explanation: An ORM generates much of the repetitive code that converts between objects and rows, so developers write less translation logic. But objects and relations still differ (nested collections versus separate tables, object references versus foreign keys and joins), and those differences leak through in query behaviour and schema design. ORMs reduce the impedance mismatch; they do not remove it, and they still run on a relational database.

questions.question: A résumé-style user profile is stored relationally. first_name and last_name are columns on the users table, but positions, education and contact information are not. What rule decides this?

options.text: Cardinality: once-per-user fields are columns; varying-count fields go in related tables
Data type: plain string fields become columns, while all other data types move into separate tables
Query frequency: the most frequently read fields are promoted to columns on the users table
Mutability: fields that never change after signup become columns on the main users table

questions.explanation: A first or last name appears exactly once per user, so it fits as a column. A person may have had several jobs, several periods of education, and any number of contact details: a one-to-many relationship from the user to those items. In a normalized relational schema such items go in separate tables with a foreign key back to users (or, in later SQL versions, in structured XML or JSON columns). Data type, read frequency, and mutability do not determine this; the number of values per user does.

questions.question: A résumé-style profile has one-to-many data (several positions, education entries, contact details). Which are valid ways to represent that data in a SQL database? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Normalized separate tables with a foreign key to users, the traditional approach prior to SQL:1999
Structured XML or JSON column types that the database can query and index inside
An opaque text column holding encoded JSON or XML, interpreted only by the application
Physical record pointers from each user row that application code follows to child records

questions.explanation: There are three common relational options with decreasing database involvement: separate child tables with foreign keys (the traditional normalized design); structured XML or JSON datatypes, supported to varying degrees by Oracle, IBM DB2, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and MySQL, which keep multi-valued data in one row yet remain queryable and indexable; and an opaque text column whose contents only the application understands. Application-followed physical pointers belong to the network (CODASYL) model, not to SQL.

optionExplanations.a: Separate child tables with foreign keys represent one-to-many relationships explicitly and let the database query and join them. This was the conventional relational design before structured document-valued columns became common.
optionExplanations.b: XML or JSON columns keep the nested items together in one row while still allowing supporting databases to inspect and index their contents. This trades normalized rows for document-like locality inside a relational system.
optionExplanations.c: An opaque text field can hold the entire nested representation, but the application must parse, validate, and query it itself, because the database typically cannot look inside. It is valid but gives the database the least involvement.
optionExplanations.d: SQL databases relate rows through key values resolved by joins at query time, not through physical pointers that application code traverses. Pointer chains followed by the application are the CODASYL network model's access paths, which the relational model replaced.

questions.question: A profile's nested data is encoded as JSON or XML and stored in a plain text column, rather than in a structured XML or JSON column type. What do you typically lose?

options.text: The database typically cannot query for values inside that column
You lose transactional guarantees on writes, since text columns bypass the log
You lose the ability to replicate that column to followers
You lose the ability to update the column after it is first written

questions.explanation: To the database, a plain text column is just a string, so it cannot interpret the structure: you typically cannot use the database to query for or index values inside that encoded column. Filtering on, say, a job title inside the encoded value must then happen in application code after fetching the whole value. Transactions, replication, and updates still work on the column like on any other value; what disappears is the database's visibility into the contents.

questions.question: Why is a JSON document a good fit for representing a résumé-style user profile?

options.text: JSON enforces a schema, so every stored profile is guaranteed to have the same fields
JSON documents support joins natively, so references between profiles resolve automatically
The profile is mostly self-contained: a tree of one-to-many data usually loaded together
A profile consists mostly of many-to-many links, which JSON nesting represents directly

questions.explanation: A résumé is mostly a self-contained document: positions, education, and contact details belong to one user and are typically read together, so nesting them in one JSON document matches the data's shape and gives one-query retrieval. JSON also has the appeal of being much simpler than XML. JSON itself enforces no schema and has no joins, and many-to-many links are exactly what nesting handles poorly. Document databases such as MongoDB, RethinkDB, CouchDB, and Espresso support this model.

questions.question: Some developers feel that a JSON document model reduces the impedance mismatch between application code and the storage layer. Which caveats qualify that view? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: JSON has problems as an encoding format, apart from its merits as a model
Its lack of a schema is often cited as an advantage, which is debatable
JSON cannot represent nested structures beyond two levels deep
JSON is not supported by any of the major relational databases

questions.explanation: JSON's nested model may reduce the object-relational impedance mismatch, but that is separate from JSON's weaknesses as a wire encoding. Also, schema flexibility is a trade-off rather than an unconditional advantage: less enforcement can simplify evolution while moving validation responsibility into application code.

optionExplanations.a: JSON's usefulness as a nested data model is separate from its wire-format limitations, such as ambiguity around numbers and binary data. Reduced impedance mismatch therefore does not imply a perfect encoding.
optionExplanations.b: Schema flexibility moves enforcement from the database toward readers and application code. That can ease heterogeneous evolution, but it can also permit inconsistent records, so calling it an unconditional advantage is debatable.
optionExplanations.c: JSON arrays and objects can be nested to arbitrary practical depths; it has no two-level structural limit. Deep nesting may be inconvenient, but it is not a format prohibition.
optionExplanations.d: Major relational databases support JSON or XML columns and functions, with varying indexing and validation capabilities. Lack of relational support is therefore not a valid caveat.

questions.question: Compare fetching a whole user profile stored as normalized relational tables (users, positions, education, contact info) with fetching it stored as one JSON document.

options.text: Relational needs multiple queries or a messy multiway join; JSON needs one
Each needs exactly one query; only the shape of the returned result differs
JSON needs more queries, since nested items resolve separately
Relational needs one join; JSON needs a follow-up query for each nested array

questions.explanation: A JSON document can place an entire profile in one record, avoiding several relational queries or a large join. That locality helps only when reads need much of the document; loading or rewriting a large document for one small field can erase the advantage.

questions.question: Why do the one-to-many relationships in a résumé-style profile (user to positions, education, contact info) form a tree, and what does a JSON representation do with that structure?

options.text: Each item has one parent and no cross-links; JSON nesting makes that tree explicit
JSON can only represent trees, so the data is reshaped to fit; the tree is a format artifact
Foreign keys among the profile tables form cycles, which JSON then flattens into a tree
The profile is read strictly top to bottom, so JSON stores it as an ordered list instead

questions.explanation: In a one-to-many relationship each child (a position, an education entry) has exactly one parent, the profile, and nothing links children sideways, so the data has a root with branches: a tree. JSON's nested objects and arrays express that tree directly, putting each child inside its parent. The tree comes from the shape of the relationships, not from the format; data with many-to-many links would not form a tree no matter how it was encoded.

questions.question: A profile stores region_id and industry_id as IDs into standardized lists (chosen from a drop-down or autocompleter) rather than as free-text strings. Which advantages does this bring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent style and spelling, and no ambiguity when places share a name
Ease of updating — the name lives in one place, so a rename propagates
Localization support — standardized lists can be translated with the site
A smaller storage footprint, which is the main motivation for using IDs

questions.explanation: Stable IDs backed by standardized lists support consistent spelling, disambiguation, localization, centralized renaming, and broader search—for example, matching a region through a city inside it. Avoiding duplicated names and meanings is the main goal, not saving a few bytes.

optionExplanations.a: Selecting a canonical place or industry produces consistent spelling and distinguishes different places with the same display name. Free-text strings cannot reliably provide that identity.
optionExplanations.b: An ID references one canonical record, so changing its displayed name updates every profile that points to it. Duplicated strings would require finding and rewriting every copy.
optionExplanations.c: A stable identifier can map to different translated labels without changing the stored relationship. This separates identity from presentation language.
optionExplanations.d: IDs may save some bytes, but storage reduction is not the main reason for normalization. Consistency, unambiguous identity, centralized updates, localization, and better search are the important benefits.

questions.question: When a record could either store an ID referencing a standardized entry or store the human-readable name directly, what is the underlying issue that decides between them?

options.text: Performance: integer IDs are faster to compare and to index than strings
Duplication: an ID stores the meaning once; text duplicates it per record
Storage: IDs consume far fewer bytes than human-readable names
Security: IDs hide business meaning from anyone reading the data

questions.explanation: The choice is fundamentally about duplication. With an ID, the human-meaningful information (such as the word Philanthropy) is stored in only one place and every record refers to it; storing the name directly duplicates that information in every record that uses it, so any later change requires updating every copy. Speed, byte size, and hiding meaning are secondary effects, not the core issue.

questions.question: In a normalized schema, why is a meaningless ID more stable than a human-readable value such as a city name?

options.text: Because an ID means nothing to humans, it never needs to change
Because IDs are assigned by the database, which never alters values
Because IDs are indexed, and index entries cannot be modified in place
Because IDs are globally unique across every system that shares them

questions.explanation: Because an ID has no meaning to humans, there is never a reason to change it: the ID can stay the same even when the information it identifies changes (for example, a city is renamed). Anything meaningful to humans may need to change someday, and if it is duplicated, every redundant copy must be updated, which incurs write overhead and risks inconsistency. The stability comes from the ID's lack of meaning, not from who assigns it or how it is indexed.

questions.question: What is the key idea behind normalization in databases?

options.text: Removing duplication of values that could be stored in just one place
Reaching at least third normal form, which is mandatory for correctness
Selectively duplicating data so that reads avoid joins under load
Enforcing an explicit schema at write time on every table

questions.explanation: Normalization means storing each piece of information in one canonical place and referring to it (for example, by ID) instead of copying it into every record. A rule of thumb: if you are duplicating values that could be stored in just one place, the schema is not normalized. The formal normal forms refine this idea, but their distinctions are of little practical interest. Selective duplication for read speed is denormalization, the opposite, and schema enforcement is a separate concept.

questions.question: Why does normalizing repeated organization or region names into referenced records fit document databases poorly?

options.text: Because document databases cannot store identifiers as references
Because normalization requires the fixed schema documents lack
It creates many-to-one relationships, and document join support is weak
Because document databases offer no secondary indexes to resolve references with

questions.explanation: Normalization replaces duplicated text with many-to-one references. That shape requires joins to recover the referenced information, while document databases are strongest when related data forms a self-contained tree and their join support is limited or product-specific.

questions.question: A profile references a region and an industry by ID, but the document database has no joins. What do you do, and why is this case forgiving?

options.text: Emulate the join in application code; the small, stable lists can be cached
Denormalize the names into each profile, which needs no extra work on renames
Change database, since there is no workaround in application code at all
Rely on the database to resolve the IDs automatically when documents are read

questions.explanation: Without database joins, the join is emulated in application code: fetch the profile, then look up the region and industry names by ID with further queries, or from an in-memory copy. This case is forgiving because the lists of regions and industries are probably small and slow-changing enough for the application to keep in memory. The work of the join has still moved from the database to the application rather than disappearing. Denormalizing the names into every profile would avoid the lookup, but then a rename has to update every copy, which is exactly the duplication that IDs exist to prevent.

questions.question: What commonly makes an initially suitable document model become awkward as an application grows?

options.text: New features add more relationships between separate documents
Documents gradually shrink into smaller, simpler trees
Data volume grows, and large nested documents cannot be partitioned across nodes
Old documents stop matching the schema enforced on write

questions.explanation: New features tend to introduce links between previously separate entities. Growing data volume alone is not the problem, and document databases typically enforce no schema on write. A document model can be an excellent initial fit for self-contained records, but increasing relationship density may make graph or relational querying more natural.

questions.question: In a résumé application, one user writes a recommendation for another, and it is displayed with the recommender's name and photo. Why should the recommendation hold a reference to the recommender's profile rather than a copy of the name and photo?

options.text: Because copies of images consume considerably more disk space
Because resolving a reference is faster than reading an inline copy
Because a photo update must show up in every past recommendation
Because the document model forbids duplicating another document's fields

questions.explanation: If the recommender later updates their photo, every recommendation they have written should show the new photo. A reference to the recommender's profile achieves that automatically, because the current photo is looked up when the recommendation is displayed; a copy would freeze the old photo and require finding and updating every copy. This is how new features turn a self-contained document into one with many-to-many relationships that need joins.

questions.question: What is true of IBM's IMS? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It was the most popular database for business data processing in the 1970s
It was built for stock-keeping in the Apollo program, released commercially in 1968
It was still in use and maintained at the time of writing, on OS/390 on IBM mainframes
It was the first commercial database to implement the SQL language

questions.explanation: IBM's Information Management System (IMS) was the most popular database for 1970s business data processing, originated in stock-keeping for the Apollo space program, was first released commercially in 1968, and was still maintained and running on IBM mainframes at the time of writing. It used the hierarchical model, a tree of records nested within records much like JSON documents, and it predates SQL, which came from the relational model. IMS worked well for one-to-many data but made many-to-many relationships difficult and had no joins.

optionExplanations.a: IMS dominated business data processing in the 1970s, showing that hierarchical databases were commercially important rather than a minor precursor. Its popularity is part of why its limitations shaped later database design.
optionExplanations.b: IMS originated in stock-keeping for the Apollo space program and became commercially available in 1968. Inventory is naturally tree-shaped, which suits its hierarchical record structure.
optionExplanations.c: IMS continued to be maintained and used on IBM mainframes running OS/390 long after relational systems became dominant. An old system can stay deployed for decades when critical applications depend on it.
optionExplanations.d: IMS uses a hierarchical model and queried data through imperative code; it predates SQL, which arose with the relational model. Confusing its commercial importance with relational innovation mixes two database generations.

questions.question: What is the network model's other name, who standardized it, and what structural change distinguishes it from the hierarchical model?

options.text: CODASYL, by the Conference on Data Systems Languages; multiple parents
CODASYL, standardized by ANSI; records were permitted to have no parent at all
The relational model, standardized by IBM; records became formally unordered
The graph model, standardized by the W3C; records acquired type labels

questions.explanation: The network model was standardized by the Conference on Data Systems Languages (CODASYL), hence its other name, the CODASYL model. It generalized the hierarchical model: in a hierarchy every record has exactly one parent, whereas a network-model record could have multiple parents. For example, one 'Greater Seattle Area' region record could be linked from every user who lived there, which allowed many-to-one and many-to-many relationships to be modeled.

questions.question: In the CODASYL network model, how did links between records differ from relational foreign keys, and what was an access path?

options.text: Links were pointer-like, stored on disk; the access path is the chain you must follow
Links were indexed foreign keys; the access path is a plan chosen by the optimizer
Links were symbolic record names; the access path is a sorted secondary index
Links were content hashes; the access path is the partition key used for routing

questions.explanation: Network-model links were not foreign-key values resolved by a query; they were more like pointers in a programming language, though stored on disk. The only way to reach a record was to follow a path from a root record along chains of these links, and that path was called an access path. Because several paths could lead to the same record in a many-to-many world, programmers had to track access paths themselves, unlike a relational optimizer choosing a plan automatically.

questions.question: How was a query performed in the CODASYL network model?

options.text: By moving a cursor through the database, iterating over records along access paths
By submitting a declarative query and letting the optimizer select the access path
By writing SQL with recursive common table expressions that follow the stored links
By issuing map and reduce functions that the framework runs across the record chains

questions.explanation: A CODASYL query was imperative: application code (typically COBOL) moved a cursor through the database, iterating over lists of records one at a time and following the links of an access path. If a record had several parents, the application had to keep track of all those relationships itself; even CODASYL committee members likened it to navigating an n-dimensional data space. Optimizer-chosen plans and recursive SQL came with the relational model, and MapReduce is much later.

questions.question: In the hierarchical and network (CODASYL) models, what was the best argument for manual access path selection, and what was its main drawback?

options.text: For: best use of 1970s hardware, notably slow tape seeks. Against: inflexible code
For: it was strictly more expressive. Against: it ran slower than SQL did
For: it guaranteed consistency. Against: it could not scale to many machines
For: it was easier for COBOL programmers to learn. Against: poor tooling

questions.explanation: Hand-chosen access paths could make the most efficient use of very limited 1970s hardware, such as tape drives whose seeks were extremely slow. The drawback was that query and update code became complicated and inflexible: if you lacked a path to the data you wanted, you had to change the access paths and rewrite a lot of handwritten query code, making the application's data model hard to change. The relational model traded that hand-tuning for an optimizer, making new features easier to add.

questions.question: Compared with CODASYL's application-managed access paths, which freedoms did the relational model introduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data is exposed as flat relations rather than nested records with application-visible traversal paths
Queries may select any rows matching a condition rather than following one predeclared access path
Applications can query by arbitrary columns, while the optimizer chooses indexes and access paths
Every insert must use a mandatory foreign-key path chosen by the application

questions.explanation: The relational model exposes tables and predicates while leaving physical access paths to the query optimizer. Foreign-key constraints may be used, but they are not the defining mechanism and applications do not manually navigate pointer chains.

optionExplanations.a: Relations expose rows and columns rather than application-visible pointer chains through nested records. That abstraction lets physical layout change without rewriting traversal code.
optionExplanations.b: A declarative predicate can select every row satisfying a condition without naming one predeclared route to each record. The engine is free to choose how to find the matches.
optionExplanations.c: Applications can filter or join on different columns, while indexes and join orders are selected by the optimizer. New access patterns therefore need not be hard-coded as cursor movements.
optionExplanations.d: Foreign keys are optional integrity constraints, not mandatory application-managed traversal paths for insertion. Requiring such navigation would recreate the CODASYL coupling the relational model removed.

questions.question: In what sense does a relational database still have access paths, and what is the big difference from CODASYL?

options.text: Index and join-order choices are the access path, made by the optimizer, not you
Relational engines dropped access paths entirely when SQL arrived
Access paths are declared in the schema and fixed for good when the table is created
Access paths are selected by the client driver before the query is sent

questions.explanation: When a relational query runs, the query optimizer decides which parts to execute in which order and which indexes to use; those choices are effectively the access path. The difference is that the optimizer makes them automatically, not the application developer. So to query data in a new way you can declare a new index and queries will use it where appropriate, without being rewritten, which made it much easier to add new features than with hand-coded CODASYL paths.

questions.question: Relational query optimizers are complex and consumed many years of research and development. Why was building one still the better trade-off than hand-coding access paths in each application?

options.text: You build the optimizer once and every application using the database benefits
Optimizers were cheap to build compared with the application code they replaced
Optimizers let the same workload run on considerably cheaper hardware
Optimizers removed the need to maintain secondary indexes by hand

questions.explanation: Hand-coding one access path may be easier than building a general optimizer, but an optimizer's cost is paid once by the database vendor and its benefits are reused by every application and query. The abstraction amortizes sophisticated planning across many users.

questions.question: In what one aspect did document databases revert to the hierarchical model, and in what respect are they not different from relational databases?

options.text: They reverted fully, access paths included, and so differ from relational entirely
They reverted in query style, becoming imperative rather than declarative
Only in nesting records within a parent; cross-references work the same in both
They reverted in ordering, making stored records position-dependent again

questions.explanation: Document databases went back to the hierarchical model in one respect: they store nested one-to-many records (such as a profile's positions and education) inside their parent record instead of in separate tables. For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships they work like relational databases: the related item is referenced by a unique identifier (a foreign key in the relational model, a document reference in the document model) and resolved at read time with a join or follow-up queries. They did not adopt CODASYL-style access paths, imperative navigation, or position-dependent records.

questions.question: Which differences between relational and document databases are properties of particular systems rather than of the relational and document data models themselves?

options.text: Fault-tolerance properties and handling of concurrency
Schema flexibility and locality of nested data
Support for joins and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships
Whether one-to-many records are nested inside a parent record

questions.explanation: Comparisons of data models concern shape: schema flexibility, locality of nested records, closeness to application data structures, and support for joins and many-to-one or many-to-many relationships. Fault tolerance (replication, failure handling) and concurrency (transactions, isolation) are separate design dimensions; systems using either data model can make very different choices about them, so they must be compared system by system rather than model by model.

questions.question: Which arguments favour the document model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema flexibility: records need not all share one structure
Better performance due to locality
For some applications, closeness to the application's own data structures
Better support for joins and many-to-many relationships

questions.explanation: The main arguments for the document model are schema flexibility, better performance due to locality (a whole aggregate in one place), and, for some applications, closeness to the nested data structures the application already uses. The relational model counters with better support for joins and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, which are exactly the shapes document models handle worst.

optionExplanations.a: Documents can accommodate records with varying fields and nested shapes without first migrating every row to one rigid structure. That flexibility helps when data is heterogeneous or externally controlled.
optionExplanations.b: Keeping a self-contained aggregate in one document can fetch it with one read instead of several joins. The benefit is conditional: it weakens when only a small portion of a large document is needed.
optionExplanations.c: For applications already manipulating nested objects, a document can closely match the in-memory shape and reduce object-relational translation. This is strongest for tree-like, self-contained records.
optionExplanations.d: Joins and many-to-many relationships are strengths of the relational model, not the document model. Documents often require denormalization or application-side joins for those relationship shapes.

questions.question: In relational schema design, what is shredding, and when does it cause problems?

options.text: Splitting a document-like tree into several tables; costly when the tree is loaded whole
Compressing documents before storing them; costly only when the CPU is the bottleneck
Partitioning documents across machines; costly only when the dataset is very small
Stripping unused fields from documents; costly when older readers still expect those fields

questions.explanation: Shredding is the relational technique of splitting a document-like structure (for example, a profile's positions, education, and contact info) across multiple tables. When the data really is a tree of one-to-many relationships and the whole tree is typically loaded at once, shredding leads to cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code that must reassemble the tree, which is when a document model is probably the better fit.

questions.question: What is the document model's limitation on referring to nested items, and under what condition does it usually not matter?

options.text: You cannot address a nested item directly, only positionally; fine if nesting is shallow
Nested items cannot be indexed at all, so every lookup scans whole documents
Nested items must first be given globally unique IDs before any query can reach them
Nested items are limited to three levels of depth by the storage format

questions.explanation: You cannot refer directly to an item nested inside a document; instead you say something like 'the second item in the list of positions for user 251', much like an access path in the hierarchical model. As long as documents are not too deeply nested, that positional style of reference is not usually a problem; it becomes awkward when deep nesting forces long paths to reach the data.

questions.question: For which kind of application is a document database's poor support for joins unlikely to matter?

options.text: An analytics application recording which events occurred at which time
A social network, because friendship edges are always symmetric
An e-commerce catalogue, because products are independent of one another
A banking ledger, because its transactions are strictly append-only

questions.explanation: An analytics application that records which events occurred at which time may never need many-to-many relationships: each event is a self-contained record, so there is nothing to join. Whether weak join support matters depends on the relationships in the data; social networks, catalogues linked to sellers and reviews, and ledgers linking accounts all involve references between records that eventually need joins, regardless of symmetry or append-only writes.

questions.question: If your application does use many-to-many relationships, which two workarounds exist in a document model, and at what cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Denormalize to avoid joins — but the application must keep copies consistent
Emulate joins in application code — usually slower than the database's own
Adopt a graph query language inside the document database itself
Store every relationship as a positional reference into the parent document

questions.explanation: With many-to-many relationships a document model offers two workarounds. You can denormalize, copying related data into each document so reads need no join, but then application code must keep all the copies consistent when the source changes. Or you can emulate joins in application code by making multiple requests to the database, which moves complexity into the application and is usually slower than a join performed by specialized code inside the database. Either way the result can be significantly more complex code and worse performance.

optionExplanations.a: Duplicating related data inside documents can make reads local, but every copy must be updated consistently when the source changes. The avoided join is exchanged for write coordination and inconsistency risk.
optionExplanations.b: Application code can fetch referenced documents and combine them, but this adds round trips and executes less specialized join logic. Database-native joins usually have more optimization opportunities.
optionExplanations.c: A particular product might add graph-like operators, but that is not a general document-model workaround and effectively introduces another query model. The two stated choices are denormalization or application-side joining.
optionExplanations.d: Positional references are fragile because inserting or reordering elements changes positions, and they recreate application-managed access paths. Stable IDs are needed for durable cross-document relationships.

questions.question: For highly interconnected data, how do the document, relational and graph models rank?

options.text: Document awkward, relational acceptable, graph most natural
Graph awkward, document acceptable, relational most natural
All three are equally suitable for interconnected data
Relational awkward, graph acceptable, document most natural

questions.explanation: For highly interconnected data, the document model is awkward (it needs denormalization or application-side joins), the relational model is acceptable (joins handle many-to-many, though variable-length traversals become clumsy), and graph models are the most natural, since edges between arbitrary vertices are their basic building block. In general no model always gives simpler code; it depends on the kinds of relationships between data items.

questions.question: Which statement accurately compares schema enforcement for document stores and relational JSON or XML columns?

options.text: Most document stores and relational JSON enforce none; relational XML may validate
Document stores validate on write; relational JSON columns are checked only on read
Relational JSON columns validate against the table schema; document stores do not
Relational XML columns cannot be validated; document stores enforce a declared schema

questions.explanation: Most document databases, and the JSON support in relational databases, do not enforce any schema on the data in documents, so arbitrary keys and values can be written and readers get no guarantee about which fields exist. XML support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation. So the accurate picture is no enforcement for documents and relational JSON, and validation that is available but optional for relational XML; neither family validates JSON against the table schema by default, and document stores do not require a declared schema.

questions.question: Why is 'schemaless' the wrong word, and what are the two accurate terms?

options.text: Code still assumes a structure, so it is implicit: schema-on-read vs schema-on-write
All databases have schemas anyway, so the right terms are strict-schema and loose-schema
Schemas live in the client driver, so the terms are client-schema and server-schema
The word is trademarked, so the accepted terms are flexible and rigid

questions.explanation: 'Schemaless' is misleading because the code that reads the data usually assumes some structure: there is an implicit schema, it is just not enforced by the database. Schema-on-read means structure is implicit and only interpreted when data is read; schema-on-write is the traditional relational approach, where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms. The schema does not disappear, it relocates.

questions.question: Map schema-on-read and schema-on-write onto programming language type checking. Which is better?

options.text: Read is dynamic runtime checking, write is static compile-time; no right answer
Read is static typing and write is dynamic typing; static checking always wins out
The closer analogy is manual versus automatic memory management
Both map to dynamic typing, since no database checks field types before a write

questions.explanation: Schema-on-read resembles dynamic runtime checking because interpretation happens when data is consumed; schema-on-write resembles static checking because structure is enforced before storage. Neither is universally better: the choice depends on data uniformity, ownership, and how safely change can be coordinated.

questions.question: Users' full names are stored in one field, and you now want first and last name stored separately. How would you typically handle this in a document database?

options.text: Write new documents with the new fields and handle old ones in read code
Run a bulk migration that rewrites every existing document in place
Declare a new schema version and reindex the whole collection
Drop the collection and recreate it with the new field layout

questions.explanation: With schema-on-read, you simply start writing new documents with first_name and last_name, and application code handles old documents when they are read (for example, splitting name if first_name is missing). No migration has to run first; the read path absorbs the mix of old and new formats. A relational database with schema-on-write would typically run ALTER TABLE to add the column and an UPDATE to fill it.

questions.question: Relational schema changes have a reputation for being slow and requiring downtime. How deserved was that reputation at the time of writing (around 2017), and what was the notable exception?

options.text: Not entirely: most ran ALTER TABLE in milliseconds, but MySQL copied the whole table
Fully deserved: every relational database rewrote the whole table on any schema change
It applied only to PostgreSQL, whose ALTER TABLE copied every row into a fresh table
It was obsolete: schema changes were instantaneous on every relational database

questions.explanation: Most relational systems executed an ALTER TABLE such as adding a column in a few milliseconds. MySQL was the notable exception at the time of writing: it copied the entire table on ALTER TABLE, which could mean minutes or hours of downtime on a large table, although tools such as pt-online-schema-change and gh-ost worked around it (later MySQL versions added online and instant DDL for many changes). The genuinely slow part of a migration is usually rewriting every row with an UPDATE.

questions.question: A relational migration adds a first_name column with ALTER TABLE and then fills it with an UPDATE over every row. Which step is the real performance problem on a large table, and what is the escape hatch?

options.text: ALTER TABLE; the escape hatch is to put the new column in a separate table
UPDATE, since every row is rewritten; leave the default NULL and fill on read
ALTER TABLE and UPDATE cost the same, and the rewrite is unavoidable
On contemporary server hardware the cost of either is negligible

questions.explanation: Adding a column with ALTER TABLE is usually quick, but an UPDATE that fills it must rewrite every row, which is slow on a large table in any database. If that is unacceptable, the application can leave first_name at its default of NULL and fill it in when a row is read, exactly as it would with a document database. The escape hatch is thus to adopt a schema-on-read style inside a relational database.

questions.question: When is data heterogeneous enough that schema-on-read is genuinely advantageous? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Many different types of object, impractical to give each its own table
Structure determined by external systems you do not control, which may change
The dataset has grown too large for the database to index efficiently
The team lacks the SQL expertise to maintain an explicit schema

questions.explanation: Schema-on-read helps when records in a collection do not all share one structure: when there are many different types of object and a table per type is impractical, or when the structure is determined by external systems you do not control and which may change at any time. In those cases a schema may hurt more than it helps. Where all records are expected to share a structure, a schema is a useful way to document and enforce it, whatever the data's size or the team's skills.

optionExplanations.a: When a collection contains many genuinely different object types, a table per type may become unwieldy and sparse common tables may misrepresent them. Interpreting each record according to its own shape can then be simpler.
optionExplanations.b: Externally controlled producers can change fields without coordinating a database migration. Schema-on-read lets consumers interpret multiple versions, though they must still validate what they receive.
optionExplanations.c: Dataset size affects indexing strategy and partitioning, not whether records share a stable structure. A large uniform dataset can still benefit from an explicit schema.
optionExplanations.d: Team familiarity with SQL is a staffing issue rather than evidence that the data is heterogeneous. Avoiding schema because of missing expertise sacrifices documentation and validation without fixing the underlying skills gap.

questions.question: Physically, why does a document stored in a document database have good locality for reading the whole record, and what is the relational contrast?

options.text: Documents are cached in memory by default, whereas rows are read from disk each time
Documents are compressed on disk, so fewer bytes cross the storage bus
A document is one continuous string; split tables need several index lookups
Documents need no index, since the whole collection is read sequentially

questions.explanation: A document is usually stored as a single continuous string, encoded as JSON, XML, or a binary variant such as MongoDB's BSON. If the application needs the whole document, for example to render a profile page, one contiguous read retrieves it. When the same data is split across several tables, multiple index lookups are needed, which may require more disk seeks and take more time. Documents still use indexes and still live on disk; the advantage is contiguity, not avoiding storage.

questions.question: A document database's locality advantage comes with conditions and costs. Which of these apply, and shape how documents should be designed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The advantage applies only if you need large parts of the document at once
The whole document is loaded even for a small portion, wasteful when large
Updates usually rewrite the whole document, so keep documents small
Locality only pays off on SSDs, not on spinning disks with slow seeks

questions.explanation: Locality helps only when a read needs a large portion of the document. Reading one field may still load the whole object, and size-changing updates often rewrite it, so documents should remain small and avoid unbounded growth. These costs substantially narrow the workloads that benefit.

optionExplanations.a: Locality helps when a request needs much of the aggregate because one contiguous document read replaces several lookups or joins. If only one field is needed, reading the rest becomes waste.
optionExplanations.b: Many document stores load the complete encoded document even for a small requested portion. Large documents therefore amplify I/O, parsing, and memory costs for narrow reads.
optionExplanations.c: Changing a document's encoded size often requires rewriting it, so frequently growing or very large documents make updates expensive. Keeping aggregates bounded preserves the intended locality benefit.
optionExplanations.d: Locality also matters on spinning disks, where avoiding seeks can be especially valuable; it is not an SSD-only effect. Hardware changes the magnitude, not the existence, of the trade-off.

questions.question: Grouping related data for locality is not unique to document databases. Match each system to its locality mechanism: Google Spanner, Oracle, Bigtable.

options.text: Spanner: interleaved child rows; Oracle: multi-table index clusters; Bigtable: column families
All three achieve locality by nesting JSON documents inside a parent document stored as one string
Spanner uses column families, Bigtable interleaves child rows, and Oracle stores whole documents
Spanner uses multi-table index clusters, Oracle column families, Bigtable interleaved rows

questions.explanation: Spanner offers document-like locality in a relational model by letting the schema declare that a table's rows are interleaved (nested) within a parent table. Oracle provides the same through multi-table index cluster tables, and the column-family concept in the Bigtable data model (also used in Cassandra and HBase) similarly manages which data is stored together. Locality is a storage-layout decision available to several models, not a property exclusive to documents.

questions.question: At the time of writing (around 2017), how far had relational databases adopted XML and JSON document support?

options.text: XML since mid-2000s except MySQL; JSON in PostgreSQL 9.3, MySQL 5.7, DB2 10.5
XML since the mid-1990s in every system; JSON only in PostgreSQL, and only as plain text
Relational databases dropped XML support once JSON became popular for web APIs
MySQL led on XML support, while PostgreSQL still has no JSON type

questions.explanation: Most relational databases other than MySQL had supported XML since the mid-2000s, including local modifications and indexing and querying inside XML documents. JSON support of a similar level existed in PostgreSQL since 9.3, MySQL since 5.7, and IBM DB2 since 10.5, with other databases expected to follow given JSON's popularity for web APIs. This let relational systems offer data models close to a document database's, which is part of the convergence of the two families.

questions.question: As document and relational databases converge, what relational-style capability were document databases adding, and what caveat applies?

options.text: RethinkDB has joins and MongoDB drivers resolve references — but client-side, so slower
Complete SQL support, built into the server, at no measurable performance cost
Enforced schemas on every collection, which then removes the need for joins at all
They are adding nothing; convergence between the families runs one way only

questions.explanation: RethinkDB supports relational-like joins in its query language, and some MongoDB drivers automatically resolve database references. A driver-side resolution is effectively a client-side join: it needs additional network round-trips and is less optimized than a join inside the database, so it is usually slower. Document databases were not adding full SQL or mandatory schemas; the convergence was in joins and references.

questions.question: Relational and document databases have been adding each other's features. Is that convergence desirable, and why is nesting values inside a relational row not a new idea?

options.text: The two families are diverging, exactly as Codd's paper predicted they would
Convergence is a mistake that dilutes the strengths of both models
It is good, and Codd's nonsimple domains already allowed nested relations
Codd forbade nested values, which makes convergence a genuine modern invention

questions.explanation: The convergence is a good thing because the models complement each other: a database that handles document-like data and also performs relational queries lets applications use whichever combination fits. Nesting is a return rather than an invention because Codd's original description already allowed nonsimple domains, where a value in a row could itself be a nested relation, forming a tree much like JSON or XML support added to SQL over 30 years later. A hybrid of the two models is a good route for databases.

questions.question: Besides a new data model, what did the relational model introduce for querying, in contrast with IMS and CODASYL?

options.text: Declarative querying via SQL, where IMS and CODASYL used imperative APIs
Transactions, which neither IMS nor CODASYL provided in any form
Indexes, where IMS and CODASYL relied on scanning every record
Replication, where IMS and CODASYL were strictly single-node systems

questions.explanation: The relational model came with declarative querying through SQL, whereas IMS and CODASYL were queried with imperative code, typically COBOL that iterated over records one at a time and followed links. With a declarative language the application states what data it wants and the database decides how to retrieve it, which is what makes an automatic query optimizer possible.

questions.question: What distinguishes an imperative query language from a declarative one?

options.text: Imperative orders operations; declarative states the pattern wanted, not the how
Imperative languages are compiled; declarative languages are interpreted
Imperative languages use loops; declarative languages use recursion instead
Imperative languages are statically typed; declarative languages are untyped

questions.explanation: A declarative language specifies what conditions the results must meet and how it should be transformed, leaving the query optimizer to decide how. 'What, not how' is the dividing line, and the optimizer is what the gap makes room for.

questions.question: A declarative query language has one obvious advantage and one more important, structural one. What is the structural one?

options.text: That it is more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API
That it hides engine internals, so queries speed up without being changed
That it is considerably easier to teach to new engineers
That queries can be type-checked statically before they ever reach the database

questions.explanation: Declarative queries are typically more concise and easier to work with, which is the obvious advantage. The more important, structural one is that a declarative language hides the implementation details of the database engine: because a query states only the result it wants, the database can introduce new indexes, storage layouts, or execution strategies and make queries faster without any change to them. Static checking and ease of teaching are not what distinguish declarative from imperative interfaces.

questions.question: A database holding a table of animal records wants to reclaim unused disk space by moving records around, which changes the order in which records come back. Why is this safe for a SQL query but risky for imperative code that iterates over the records?

options.text: SQL promises no order, but imperative code might rely on the order it saw
SQL locks the table during compaction, while imperative code reads concurrently
SQL reads through an index, while imperative code reads the raw disk layout
SQL keeps records in insertion order, while imperative code sorts them itself

questions.explanation: A SQL query without ORDER BY guarantees no particular ordering, so it does not mind if the order changes. With imperative code that loops over the records, the database can never be sure whether the code relies on their order. SQL being more limited in functionality gives the database far more room for automatic optimizations such as compaction. Locks and the code's access to disk layout are beside the point; the issue is what the query's semantics promise.

questions.question: Which hardware trend favours declarative languages, and what argument follows?

options.text: CPUs gain cores, not clock speed; imperative ordering resists parallelism
Disks are getting faster, so the choice of query plan matters much less
Memory is getting cheaper, so datasets fit in RAM and query plans stop mattering
Networks are getting faster, which favours joins on the client side

questions.explanation: Processor performance increasingly grows through additional cores rather than much faster single cores. A declarative query specifies the desired result without fixing execution order, giving the engine freedom to partition and parallelize work across those cores.

questions.question: In CSS, the selector written as li.selected, then the child combinator (a greater-than sign), then p matches which elements?

options.text: A `p` directly inside an `li.selected` element
Every `p` anywhere below any `li`, regardless of its class
Every `li` that contains a `p` somewhere among its descendants
Only the first `p` element that appears anywhere in the document

questions.explanation: The child combinator (the greater-than sign) requires a direct parent-child relationship, and .selected requires that parent li to carry the CSS class selected. So the rule matches only p elements whose direct parent is an li with class selected. Without the combinator, the descendant selector li.selected p would match a p at any depth below the selected list item. Like a SQL query, the selector declares the pattern and leaves the browser to find the matches.

questions.question: To give the p title inside the selected li a blue background, a page uses imperative JavaScript DOM code (loop over li elements, check for the selected class, set a style on each p child) instead of a declarative CSS rule. Beyond being longer, which serious problems does the JavaScript have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It doesn't undo itself — removing the class leaves the element blue until reload
It blocks engine improvements — a new DOM API means rewriting the code
It is unable to select elements by their class name at all
It runs correctly in only one particular browser rendering engine

questions.explanation: First, the imperative code applies the style once and never undoes it: if the selected class is removed, the blue background stays until the page reloads, whereas with CSS the browser automatically removes the style when the rule stops applying. Second, the code is tied to particular DOM APIs, so taking advantage of a faster API such as getElementsByClassName means rewriting it, whereas browser vendors can speed up CSS matching without breaking compatibility. That is the same argument for declarative database queries.

optionExplanations.a: Imperative JavaScript sets a style once but does not automatically reverse it when the element stops matching. Declarative CSS continuously relates appearance to the current DOM state, so removal of the class removes the rule's effect.
optionExplanations.b: Imperative code commits to a particular traversal API and algorithm, so adopting a faster new API requires code changes. A CSS engine can optimize rule evaluation internally while preserving the same declaration.
optionExplanations.c: DOM APIs can select elements by class, including `getElementsByClassName`; inability to select them is not the problem. The issue is maintaining the result and coupling code to the traversal mechanism.
optionExplanations.d: Standard DOM manipulation is not inherently limited to one rendering engine. Browser differences can exist, but the stated architectural problems are stale effects and blocked implementation optimization.

questions.question: Why is MapReduce neither fully declarative nor a conventional imperative query API?

options.text: The framework drives iteration but calls user-written imperative map and reduce code
It is declarative in exactly the same way as SQL and contains no user code
Users manually navigate every stored record and choose every access path
Its map phase is declarative while its reduce phase is always relational

questions.explanation: The framework decides how to distribute, schedule, and repeatedly invoke user functions, but the functions themselves contain executable logic. Their names come from functional programming: map is also called collect, while reduce is also called fold or inject.

questions.question: MongoDB's mapReduce command for counting shark sightings per month is given the option query: { family: 'Sharks' } alongside its JavaScript map and reduce functions. What does that option do?

options.text: It declaratively selects only shark documents, so map runs once per match
Nothing on its own: the shark filter must also be written inside the map function body
It runs after reduce, discarding the monthly totals that are not about sharks
It is applied in the reduce step, removing non-shark values from each group of keys

questions.explanation: The query option selects only documents whose family is 'Sharks', and MongoDB calls the JavaScript map function once for each matching document. Specifying the filter declaratively is a MongoDB-specific extension to MapReduce rather than logic that must be embedded in the map or reduce callback, and it happens before map, so non-shark observations never reach map or reduce.

questions.question: A MongoDB observations collection holds two shark observations from December 1995, with numAnimals of 3 and 4. A mapReduce job's map function emits the key 'year-month' with value numAnimals, and reduce sums the values. How many times are map and reduce called, and what does reduce receive?

options.text: map runs twice, emitting ('1995-12', 3) and ('1995-12', 4); reduce gets [3, 4], returns 7
map runs once for the pair, emitting ('1995-12', 7), and reduce is never called
reduce runs once per document, accumulating a running total that reaches 7
map emits 3 and 4 under separate keys, and reduce returns them unchanged

questions.explanation: Map is called once per matching document, emitting ('1995-12', 3) and ('1995-12', 4). The framework then groups the emitted key-value pairs by key, and reduce is called once for each distinct key with all of that key's values: reduce('1995-12', [3, 4]), which returns 7. Reduce does not run per document, and map does not see multiple documents at once.

questions.question: Which restriction lets a framework relocate, reorder, and retry MapReduce functions safely?

options.text: They use only their input data and produce no external side effects
They must be JavaScript functions that can freely query the database
They may perform side effects as long as each worker has a unique ID
They must be declarative expressions and cannot call library functions

questions.explanation: Pure functions depend only on their input and do not mutate external state, so rerunning one does not duplicate a side effect and moving it to another worker does not change its meaning. They may still parse strings, call libraries, and perform arbitrary calculations.

questions.question: Why did MongoDB add a declarative aggregation pipeline alongside MapReduce?

options.text: MapReduce could not distribute work, so the pipeline added worker scheduling
Coordinating two JavaScript functions is awkward; declarative stages optimize better
JavaScript support was removed, so the pipeline became the only way to read documents
MapReduce could not represent any filtering, grouping, or aggregation operation

questions.explanation: MongoDB 2.2 added the pipeline because a sequence of declarative stages is usually easier to write and optimize than two coordinated JavaScript functions. Its expressiveness resembles a subset of SQL, illustrating how useful declarative ideas reappeared in NoSQL systems.

questions.question: Using relationship shape alone, when is the document model appropriate and when does a graph become natural?

options.text: Documents fit trees or no relationships; graphs fit complex connections
Graphs fit tree-structured data; documents fit heavily interconnected data
The choice between them depends only on the total volume of data
Graphs are preferable as soon as any single many-to-many relationship appears

questions.explanation: If an application has mostly one-to-many (tree-structured) relationships or no relationships between records, the document model is appropriate. The relational model handles simple many-to-many cases, but as connections within the data become more complex, modeling the data as a graph becomes more natural. A single many-to-many relationship does not by itself require a graph; the deciding factor is how complex and pervasive the connections are, not data volume.

questions.question: A graph consists of two kinds of objects. What are they, with their common synonyms?

options.text: Vertices (nodes, entities) and edges (relationships, arcs)
Rows (also called tuples) and links (stored on-disk pointers)
Documents (also called records) and references (foreign keys)
Subjects (also called heads) and predicates (also called tails)

questions.explanation: A graph is made of vertices (also called nodes or entities) and edges (also called relationships or arcs), where each edge connects two vertices. For example, in a social graph vertices are people and edges indicate who knows whom; in the web graph vertices are pages and edges are HTML links; in a road network vertices are junctions and edges are roads. Algorithms such as shortest-path search and PageRank operate on these structures.

questions.question: In social graphs, the web graph, and road networks, every vertex represents the same kind of thing. What is that property called, and what equally powerful alternative use of graphs exists?

options.text: They are homogeneous; but graphs also store wholly different object types together
They are all directed, and a graph model cannot represent undirected edges
They are all acyclic, and the graph model requires acyclicity to work
