They are all small enough to be held entirely in main memory

questions.explanation: Those graphs are homogeneous: all vertices are people, or web pages, or road junctions. An equally powerful use is to store completely different types of objects consistently in one datastore. Facebook, for example, maintains a single graph whose vertices represent people, locations, events, check-ins, and comments, with edges for friendships, which check-in happened where, who commented on which post, and who attended which event. Direction, cycles, and memory size are not what these examples share.

questions.question: Which two graph data models are commonly contrasted?

options.text: Property graphs and triple stores
Relational graphs and document graphs
Hierarchical trees and CODASYL networks
Property graphs and adjacency matrices

questions.explanation: The two graph data models usually contrasted are the property-graph model and the triple-store model; an adjacency matrix is a storage representation, not a data model. Property-graph implementations include Neo4j, Titan, and InfiniteGraph; triple stores include Datomic and AllegroGraph. Declarative languages span Cypher for property graphs, SPARQL for RDF triples, and Datalog as a more general rule-based approach.

questions.question: What core information does an edge store in a property graph?

options.text: An ID, tail and head vertex IDs, a label, and properties
Only the two endpoint IDs, with no label or edge properties
A collection of properties with no endpoints or direction
Only a traversal weight and the label of its source vertex

questions.explanation: The tail identifies where a directed edge starts and the head where it ends; the label names the relationship and properties describe it. Vertices separately have IDs, incoming and outgoing edge references, and their own properties, with indexes enabling traversal in either direction.

questions.question: Which are the three important aspects of the property graph model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex; no schema restricts associations
From any vertex you can efficiently find incoming and outgoing edges alike
Different edge labels let one graph hold several kinds of information cleanly
Edges may only be traversed in the direction in which they were created

questions.explanation: Property graphs allow unrestricted vertex-to-vertex edges, efficient traversal in either direction, and labels that distinguish relationship types. Those properties let one graph represent heterogeneous, highly connected information without fixing one hierarchy in advance.

optionExplanations.a: Property graphs allow an edge between arbitrary vertices without a schema fixing one hierarchy. That freedom supports evolving, heterogeneous relationships such as people, places, organizations, and events.
optionExplanations.b: Indexes on both tail and head endpoints let a traversal efficiently follow outgoing or incoming edges. Direction labels the relationship but does not restrict which way a query may navigate.
optionExplanations.c: Labels distinguish relationship meanings such as `BORN_IN`, `LIVES_IN`, or `MARRIED_TO` within one graph. Queries can select the relevant type without separating every relationship into another database.
optionExplanations.d: Directed edges record a tail and head, but graph stores normally support lookup from either endpoint. Creation direction expresses semantics; it does not force all traversals to move only forward.

questions.question: A graph links people to locations (BORN_IN, LIVES_IN) and locations to larger regions (WITHIN) across several countries. Which features of such data would be difficult to express in a traditional relational schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Different regional structures per country — départements and régions versus counties and states
Quirks of history, such as a country existing within another country
Varying granularity — a residence given as a city, a birthplace only as a state
The total count of people currently represented anywhere in the graph

questions.explanation: A traditional relational schema fixes its tables and columns in advance, so it struggles with irregular structure: different regional hierarchies per country (France has départements and régions, the US counties and states), historical quirks such as a country within a country, and varying granularity (a residence given as a city but a birthplace only as a state). A graph handles these by adding vertices and WITHIN edges as needed. A simple total count of people is easy in either model.

optionExplanations.a: Administrative hierarchies differ by country, so one fixed set of nullable relational columns fits poorly and requires many exceptions. A graph can add the appropriate place types and `WITHIN` edges per region.
optionExplanations.b: Historical arrangements can violate a simple tree, such as one country being contained within another in a special sense. Flexible edges represent the exception without redesigning a universal hierarchy.
optionExplanations.c: A graph can link a person to a city in one case and only a state in another while preserving both as locations. Fixed relational levels make this variable granularity awkward.
optionExplanations.d: Counting all represented people is a straightforward aggregate over person rows or vertices. Irregular relationship structure is irrelevant to that simple global count.

questions.question: A property graph records people and where they were born and live. How would you extend it to answer 'what is safe for each person to eat', and what general property of graphs does that show?

options.text: Add allergen vertices with edges to people and foods; graphs extend easily
Add a free-text allergies property per person; graphs favour properties over edges
Move allergies into a separate relational table, since graphs cannot be extended
Encode allergies only as edge properties; edges are cheaper to add than vertices

questions.explanation: Introduce a vertex for each allergen, an edge from a person to each allergen they react to, and edges linking allergens to the foods that contain them; a query can then follow person, allergen, and food to find what is safe for each person to eat. Nothing existing has to be migrated: new vertex types and edge labels are simply added alongside the BORN_IN and LIVES_IN data. That shows that graphs are good for evolvability, because the graph can easily be extended as the application's data structures change. A free-text property would hide the relationships from queries, and graphs have no trouble being extended.

questions.question: What is Cypher, who made it, and where does the name come from?

options.text: A declarative property-graph language from Neo4j, named after a Matrix character
An imperative traversal API from Titan, named after the cryptographic term cipher
A triple-store query language standardized by the W3C for RDF data
A MapReduce dialect created at Google for graph-shaped datasets

questions.explanation: Cypher is Neo4j's declarative query language for property graphs. Its name references the character Cypher from The Matrix, not cryptography; pattern syntax states the graph shape to match while the engine chooses the traversal plan.

questions.question: In a Cypher CREATE clause, the pattern (Idaho) -[:WITHIN]→ (USA) is written with an arrow pointing from Idaho to USA. What does it create?

options.text: An edge labeled WITHIN, with Idaho as tail and USA as head
An edge labeled WITHIN, with USA as tail and Idaho as head
Two undirected edges labeled WITHIN between Idaho and USA
A property named WITHIN set on the Idaho vertex

questions.explanation: The arrow runs from Idaho to USA, so Cypher creates an edge labeled WITHIN with Idaho as the tail vertex (where the edge starts) and USA as the head vertex (where it ends): Idaho is within the USA. Edges in a property graph are directed and the label names the relationship; WITHIN is not stored as a property of either vertex. Symbolic names like Idaho let later parts of the query refer to the same vertices.

questions.question: A Cypher MATCH finds persons with a BORN_IN edge leading to a place connected by a chain of zero or more outgoing WITHIN edges to a Location named 'United States', and a LIVES_IN edge leading similarly to 'Europe'. What does it return?

options.text: Names of people who emigrated from the United States to Europe
Names of people born in Europe who now live in the United States
Names of everyone in the graph having any BORN_IN edge at all
Names of all Location vertices inside the United States and Europe

questions.explanation: The query returns the names of people who emigrated from the United States to Europe: both conditions must hold for the same person vertex, so the person must have a BORN_IN edge into some place within the United States and a LIVES_IN edge into some place within Europe. The variable-length WITHIN*0.. part follows zero or more WITHIN edges, so a birthplace or residence recorded at any granularity (city, state, region) still rolls up to the country or continent. Reversing the direction or dropping either condition gives a different set of people.

questions.question: For people and places linked by `BORN_IN`, `LIVES_IN`, and `WITHIN`, who chooses how a declarative emigration query traverses the graph?

options.text: Application code must choose depth-first or breadth-first traversal
Only a full scan of all people is possible
The optimizer chooses the starting point and traversal plan
The query must state one fixed traversal order

questions.explanation: A declarative graph query describes the required relationship pattern, not the traversal order. The optimizer can scan people or begin from indexed location vertices and walk incoming `WITHIN`, `BORN_IN`, and `LIVES_IN` edges, depending on estimated cost.

questions.question: Can you query graph data with SQL, and what is the precise reason for the difficulty?

options.text: Yes, awkwardly: a traversal needs a number of joins not fixed in advance
No: SQL cannot express traversal, so the data must move to a graph database
Yes trivially, because a join and an edge traversal are exactly equivalent
Yes, but only for undirected graphs whose edge labels are all uniform

questions.explanation: Graph data stored in vertex and edge tables can be queried with SQL, but awkwardly. In a typical relational query you know in advance which joins you need; in a graph query you may have to traverse a variable number of edges before reaching the vertex you want. A person's LIVES_IN edge may point at a street, a city, a region, or a state, and reaching the country can take one WITHIN hop or several. Since SQL:1999, recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE) can express such variable-length paths, but the query is far longer and clumsier than the equivalent Cypher pattern WITHIN*0...

questions.question: Give the form of a triple and name its three parts with an example.

options.text: (subject, predicate, object) — as in (Jim, likes, bananas)
(vertex, edge, vertex) — with the predicate left implicit
(key, value, timestamp) — as in a versioned key-value store
(table, row, column) — addressing one cell of a relation

questions.explanation: Jim is the subject, “likes” is the predicate, and bananas is the object. Triple stores express many of the same ideas as property graphs with different terminology, but their RDF ecosystem and SPARQL query language make the representation independently useful.

questions.question: The subject of a triple is a vertex. The object is one of two things. Which, and what does the predicate mean in each case? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A primitive value — then predicate and object are a property key and value, as in (lucy, age, 33)
Another vertex — then the predicate is an edge label, subject the tail, object the head
A nested triple, which is what makes the whole model recursive
A reference to an RDF document that is stored on another server

questions.explanation: In a triple-store, the object is either a primitive value or another vertex, and that choice decides what the predicate means. With a primitive value, such as (lucy, age, 33), the predicate and object are the key and value of a property on the subject vertex, like {"age":33}. With another vertex, such as (lucy, marriedTo, alain), the predicate is the label of an edge whose tail is the subject and whose head is the object. Basic triples do not nest other triples, and an object need not refer to a document on another server.

optionExplanations.a: When the object is a primitive, the predicate names an attribute and the object supplies its value. Thus `(lucy, age, 33)` corresponds to a property key-value pair on Lucy's vertex.
optionExplanations.b: When the object identifies another vertex, the predicate names the relationship; the subject is the edge tail and the object is its head. This is how triples represent graph edges.
optionExplanations.c: Basic RDF triples contain a subject, predicate, and object; an ordinary object is a value or a vertex, not another complete triple. Extensions such as RDF-star exist, but they are not part of the basic triple model.
optionExplanations.d: An object may be a URI identifying a vertex, but it need not point to a remotely stored RDF document or resolve over the network. URIs can function simply as globally unique names.

questions.question: In Turtle notation for RDF triples, what does a name written as _:someName denote, and what does a semicolon do?

options.text: A file-local vertex name; a semicolon adds more facts about the same subject
A globally unique URI that must resolve; the semicolon terminates each statement
A predicate marker; the semicolon separates one subject's triples from the next
A literal string value; the semicolon begins a trailing comment

questions.explanation: A name such as _:lucy identifies a vertex only within that file: it means nothing outside it and exists only so that several triples can refer to the same vertex. A semicolon lets you state several predicates and objects about the same subject without repeating it, which makes Turtle (a subset of Notation3, N3) compact and readable. Whether a predicate is an edge or a property is decided by the object: another vertex gives an edge, a string literal gives a property.

questions.question: State the semantic web's core idea, what RDF was for, and whether it worked.

options.text: Replace HTML with XML; RDF was a styling language; it largely succeeded
Also publish machine-readable data; RDF the common format; overhyped, unrealized
Build one global graph database; RDF was its storage engine; judged premature
Standardize SQL across websites; RDF was its wire protocol; adoption still ongoing

questions.explanation: The semantic web's idea is that websites, which already publish text and pictures for humans, should also publish machine-readable data for computers. RDF (Resource Description Framework) was meant to be the consistent format that lets data from different sites be combined automatically into a web of data, an internet-wide database of everything. It was overhyped in the early 2000s and, at the time of writing, had shown no sign of being realized in practice, partly because of overly complex standards. Useful work still came out of it: triples can be a good internal data model, and the triple-store model does not depend on the semantic web at all.

questions.question: Why are RDF subjects, predicates and objects often URIs, and must they resolve?

options.text: For internet-wide exchange: a URI predicate avoids collisions, and need not resolve
Because RDF requires every identifier to be fetchable over HTTP to be valid
Because URIs compress better than plain strings in the stored representation
Because the SPARQL grammar only accepts URIs in predicate position

questions.explanation: RDF was designed for internet-wide data exchange, so a predicate is often a URI such as http://my-company.com/namespace#within rather than just within. If you combine your data with someone else's and they attach a different meaning to within, there is no conflict, because their predicate is a different URI. The URI does not need to resolve to anything: from RDF's point of view it is simply a namespace, usually declared once as a prefix at the top of the file. Non-resolvable forms such as urn:example:within work just as well.

questions.question: What does SPARQL stand for?

options.text: SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language
Structured Parallel Query and Retrieval Language
Semantic Property And Relationship Query Language
Simple Pattern And RDF Query Layer

questions.explanation: SPARQL stands for SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language and is usually pronounced “sparkle.” It predates Cypher and influenced Cypher's declarative graph-pattern style, although SPARQL targets RDF triples while Cypher targets property graphs.

questions.question: Which statements accurately compare SPARQL with Cypher for the same graph-pattern query? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The query is even more concise in SPARQL; its variables start with a question mark
RDF uses predicates for both properties and edges, so one syntax matches both
SPARQL has no way at all to express variable-length path traversal
SPARQL requires an explicit join clause where Cypher manages without one

questions.explanation: SPARQL variables begin with `?`, and RDF represents both attributes and relationships as predicate triples, allowing one pattern syntax for both. This can make the equivalent query concise even though the underlying RDF and property-graph models differ.

optionExplanations.a: SPARQL variables use a `?` prefix, and its triple-pattern syntax can express the same relationship pattern compactly. Concision comes from matching the RDF representation directly, not from omitting semantics.
optionExplanations.b: RDF represents both an attribute and a relationship with a predicate, so the same subject-predicate-object pattern matches either. Property graphs usually distinguish vertex properties from edges more explicitly.
optionExplanations.c: SPARQL can express variable-length paths using property-path operators such as repetition. Claiming it has no path mechanism confuses basic triple patterns with the full query language.
optionExplanations.d: Adjacent SPARQL graph patterns share variables and thereby express joins without a separate `JOIN` clause. The optimizer chooses how to execute those matches just as in other declarative languages.

questions.question: Are graph databases the second coming of CODASYL in disguise? Which differences rule that out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema — CODASYL fixed which record type nests in which; graphs impose no such rule
Reaching a record — CODASYL forced path traversal; graphs allow direct ID or index lookup
Ordering — CODASYL children were an ordered set; graph vertices and edges are unordered
Storage — CODASYL wrote links to disk whereas graph databases are memory-only

questions.explanation: Graph databases are not CODASYL in disguise. CODASYL's schema fixed which record type could nest within which, while any graph vertex can have an edge to any other; CODASYL records could be reached only by traversing an access path, while graph vertices can be looked up directly by ID or through an index; and CODASYL children formed an ordered set the database had to maintain, while graph vertices and edges are unordered. A further difference is query style: CODASYL queries were imperative, whereas graph databases also offer declarative languages such as Cypher and SPARQL. Both kinds of system persist data on disk.

optionExplanations.a: CODASYL schemas fixed which record types could nest under others, while property graphs allow arbitrary vertex-to-vertex edges. That makes graph structure far easier to extend.
optionExplanations.b: CODASYL applications had to start at an access point and follow paths; graph databases can also locate a vertex directly by ID or indexed property. Traversal is an option rather than the only access mechanism.
optionExplanations.c: CODASYL child records formed an ordered set, making position part of its navigation model. Graph edges and vertices have no inherent order unless an application stores one explicitly.
optionExplanations.d: Graph databases are not memory-only; they commonly persist vertices and edges to disk just as CODASYL systems persisted records and links. Storage medium is not the differentiating feature.

questions.question: Which systems are concrete examples of Datalog use?

options.text: Datomic and Cascalog
Neo4j and Gremlin
PostgreSQL and MySQL
MongoDB and CouchDB

questions.explanation: Datalog was studied academically in the 1980s and helped establish ideas used by later query languages. Datomic uses a Clojure-style syntax, while Cascalog brings Datalog-like queries to large Hadoop datasets; Datalog itself is a restricted subset of Prolog.

questions.question: How does Datalog's notation relate to the triple-store model?

options.text: A generalization: a triple is written predicate(subject, object)
It writes each triple as subject(predicate, object) instead
It abandons triples in favour of an unrelated table-and-column notation
It writes each triple as object(subject, predicate)

questions.explanation: Datalog generalizes the triple notation as `predicate(subject, object)`. Facts and derived rules use the same form, which makes recursive relationship queries composable rather than requiring explicit traversal code.

questions.question: Cypher and SPARQL jump in right away with SELECT. What does Datalog do instead, and what is the payoff?

options.text: It compiles down to SQL, so the payoff is portability across engines
It defines rules creating new derived predicates, which can build on each other
It executes imperatively, so the payoff is precise control over traversal
It requires a schema declaration first, so the payoff is validation

questions.explanation: Datalog takes a small step at a time: rules aren't triples stored in the database but are derived from data or from other rules, and can call each other or recurse — so complex queries build up a piece at a time.

questions.question: State the convention for Datalog variables and the condition under which a rule applies.

options.text: Uppercase-initial words are variables; a rule fires when all predicates right of :- match
Variables start with a question mark; a rule fires when any right-hand predicate matches
Variables start with an underscore; rules apply unconditionally to every fact
Variables are quoted strings; rules apply only to triples already stored

questions.explanation: In Datalog rules, words starting with an uppercase letter are variables, matched against facts much like patterns in Cypher and SPARQL. A rule applies when the system can find a match for all predicates on the right-hand side of the :- operator; it is then as though the left-hand side, with variables replaced by the matched values, were added to the database. Because every right-hand predicate must match, a rule is a conjunction, and derived facts can feed further rules step by step.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of Datalog's rule-based approach to querying?

options.text: Harder for one-off queries, but reusable rules help as complexity grows
Always more convenient than SQL, and no harder to reason about at all
Faster to execute, but strictly less expressive than SQL turns out to be
Well suited to one-off queries, but unable to handle complex data at all

questions.explanation: Datalog requires a different kind of thinking: you define rules that derive new predicates and then combine and reuse them across queries. That makes it less convenient for simple one-off queries than jumping straight to a SELECT, but it copes better when the data is complex, because rules built once can be composed into larger queries. It is not universally more convenient, and it is well able to express complex recursive queries.

questions.question: Reconstruct the historical arc from the hierarchical model to NoSQL.

options.text: One big tree, then relational for many-to-many, then NoSQL splitting into document and graph
Relational first, then the hierarchical model for performance, then graph models for many-to-many links
Graphs first, then flattened into trees for speed, then normalized into relational tables for consistency
Documents first, then hierarchical trees, then relational tables as data became more regular over time

questions.explanation: Data was first represented as one big tree (the hierarchical model, as in IMS), which handled many-to-many relationships badly, so the relational model was invented to solve that. Later, developers found some applications do not fit the relational model well either, and NoSQL datastores diverged in two directions: document databases for self-contained records with rare cross-links, and graph databases where anything may relate to everything. Each transition was driven by a relationship shape the previous model handled poorly.

questions.question: Which relationship shapes favor document databases versus graph databases?

options.text: Documents fit data needing strict schemas; graphs fit data with no relationships
Documents fit interconnected data; graphs fit self-contained records
Documents fit self-contained trees; graphs fit dense, flexible relationships
Both target the same use case, differing only in query syntax

questions.explanation: Document databases favor self-contained, tree-like records whose links to other records are uncommon. Graph databases favor dense, flexible relationships where any entity may connect to many others. The useful distinction is relationship shape, not merely query syntax.

questions.question: Although relational, document, and graph models can emulate one another, why do distinct models remain useful?

options.text: Emulation is possible but awkward, e.g. graph data in relational tables
Because graph structures genuinely cannot be emulated in a relational database
Because relational databases are unable to store nested data of any kind
Because the three models offer materially different consistency guarantees

questions.explanation: Expressive equivalence does not imply equal convenience or performance. A graph can be represented in tables, but recursive traversals may be verbose; nested documents can be normalized, but reconstructing them requires joins. Each model makes different common operations natural.

questions.question: Which property do document and graph databases share, what does it buy, and what is the qualification?

options.text: Both support joins natively across records, which is what improves their storage locality
Typically no enforced schema, easing change; the application still assumes a structure
Both guarantee strong consistency on every write, which greatly simplifies application code
Both store all their data as nested trees, which is what improves their cache behaviour

questions.explanation: Document and graph databases typically do not enforce a schema on the data they store, which can make it easier to adapt applications to changing requirements. The qualification is that the application most likely still assumes the data has a certain structure; the question is only whether the schema is explicit and enforced on write, or implicit and handled on read. Graph databases are not tree-structured, and neither family is defined by joins or consistency guarantees.

questions.question: Which of these are not database query languages? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: CSS
XSL/XPath
Cypher
Datalog

questions.explanation: SQL, MapReduce, MongoDB's aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL, and Datalog query stored data. CSS and XSL/XPath are declarative styling or document-transformation languages; their inclusion is comparative, showing how declarative interfaces hide execution strategy.

optionExplanations.a: CSS declaratively selects document elements to style; it does not retrieve or transform records in a database. It is included as an analogy for letting an engine choose execution strategy.
optionExplanations.b: XSL and XPath appear in this comparison as declarative languages for selecting and transforming parts of a document, not as database query languages. XPath can query XML in other contexts, so the distinction is about the role it plays as an analogy.
optionExplanations.c: Cypher is a declarative query language for property graphs, matching vertex and edge patterns and returning stored graph data. It is therefore a database query language.
optionExplanations.d: Datalog queries stored and derived relations through logical rules, and systems such as Datomic and Cascalog use it for data access. Its rule-based syntax does not make it merely a programming language.

questions.question: Which specialized domain needs sequence-similarity search, and which system serves it?

options.text: Genome research, served by specialized software such as GenBank
Genome research, served by full-text search engines such as Lucene
Particle physics at the LHC, served by a standard relational database
Full-text search, served by the sequence-matching features of graph databases

questions.explanation: Researchers working with genome data need sequence-similarity search: taking one very long string representing a DNA molecule and matching it against a large database of strings that are similar but not identical. General-purpose relational, document, and graph databases cannot handle this kind of usage, so researchers wrote specialized genome database software such as GenBank. Full-text search matches words and terms rather than near-identical long sequences, and particle physics at the LHC needs custom solutions for its scale of hundreds of petabytes, not sequence similarity.

questions.question: Having settled on a data model, what is the next layer down to decide?

options.text: How the model is implemented: storage and retrieval on disk
How data is replicated and partitioned across many machines
Which encoding format is used and how schemas evolve over time
Which transaction isolation level the application really needs

questions.explanation: After choosing how application data is represented—relational, document, or graph—the next concern is how a storage engine lays that model out on disk and retrieves it efficiently. Replication, transactions, and encoding build on that storage foundation.
